Tumor Biology & Risk Factors.title: CNS Tumor Biology: What Is It?
Tumor Biology & Risk Factors.html:
Every CNS consult starts with one question: I see a lesion in the brain or spine. What is it, where is it, how aggressive is it, and should the radiation be focal, regional, whole-brain, or craniospinal? The six CNS readings follow that question in order. This one answers the first part: what is it?

1
What is it? (tumor biology)
→
2
Where is it? (neuroanatomy)
→
3
What does it look like? (imaging)
→
4
How do I classify it? (workup)
→
5
How do I treat it?
→
6
How do I deliver it safely?

Primary CNS Tumor or Spread to the CNS?

The first split is whether the tumor started in the CNS (gliomas, meningiomas, schwannomas, pituitary tumors, lymphoma) or spread there from a cancer elsewhere (brain and spine metastases). The two follow completely different workups and treatment logic, which the Workup reading lays out side by side.

Radiation plays an important role in many CNS tumors, benign and malignant, but the roles of surgery, systemic therapy, observation, and radiation vary a lot by tumor type, size, location, and patient factors.

The CNS 5

Five tumors cover most of what you'll see on a CNS service. Know who gets each one and why it matters.

TumorThink of it whenWhy it matters
Brain metastasesA patient with known cancer, especially lung, breast, or melanoma; often multiple lesionsThe most common intracranial tumor and the most common CNS problem on a radiation service
MeningiomaAn extra-axial mass in a middle-aged or older woman, or after prior cranial RTThe most common primary tumor; usually benign, but location can make it hard to treat
GlioblastomaAn older adult with a rapidly growing, enhancing, infiltrative massThe aggressive adult diffuse glioma; almost always recurs despite surgery, RT, and chemo
Vestibular schwannomaOne-sided hearing loss, tinnitus, or imbalance (CN VIII)Benign and slow; the decision is observe vs SRS vs surgery while protecting hearing
Primary CNS lymphomaImmunosuppression (HIV, transplant); a deep periventricular massSteroids can shrink it and ruin the biopsy; chemotherapy comes first
Clinical Pearl

Don't mix up "most common brain tumor overall" (metastases), "most common primary" (meningioma), and "most common malignant primary" (glioblastoma).

A few others round out the service: IDH-mutant gliomas (astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma) in younger adults who often present with a seizure and live much longer than patients with glioblastoma; pituitary adenomas and craniopharyngiomas under the optic chiasm; and spine metastases causing cord compression.

Reference: pediatric CNS tumors in one paragraph▾

Brain tumors are the most common solid tumor of childhood, and most arise in the posterior fossa. The ones you'll hear about: pilocytic astrocytoma (the most common pediatric glioma, often cured by surgery), medulloblastoma (the most common malignant one; spreads through CSF, so it needs craniospinal irradiation), ependymoma, and diffuse midline glioma of the pons. Children are especially vulnerable to late effects on growth, hormones, and cognition, which is why protons are often used.

Risk Factors

1
Ionizing Radiation

The only established environmental cause. Prior cranial RT raises the risk of meningioma most, then glioma, often decades later.

2
Immunosuppression

HIV and organ transplant raise the risk of EBV-driven primary CNS lymphoma.

3
Genetic Syndromes

Rare, but the tumor pattern points to the syndrome (table below).

SyndromeCNS tumors to look for
NF1Optic pathway glioma, other astrocytomas, neurofibromas
NF2Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, spinal ependymomas
Von Hippel-LindauHemangioblastoma (cerebellum, retina, spinal cord)
Reference: rarer syndromes▾
  • Li-Fraumeni (TP53): gliomas, choroid plexus carcinoma, medulloblastoma; avoid radiation when there's a reasonable alternative.
  • Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2): subependymal giant cell astrocytoma.
  • Gorlin (PTCH1): medulloblastoma; RT causes many basal cell cancers in the field.
  • Lynch / FAP: glioblastoma (Lynch) and medulloblastoma (FAP).

Classification Instead of Stage

Most brain tumors don't spread outside the CNS, so adult CNS tumors have no TNM stage. They're described by WHO tumor type and grade (1-4), and the current WHO system builds an integrated diagnosis from histology plus molecular markers.

For adult-type diffuse gliomas, IDH and 1p/19q status are the foundation:

1
IDH-mutant + 1p/19q codeleted → oligodendroglioma
→
2
IDH-mutant, no codeletion → astrocytoma
→
3
IDH-wildtype, meeting specific criteria → glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype

Not every IDH-wildtype tumor is automatically glioblastoma: it has to meet specific histologic or molecular criteria, which the Workup reading covers. MGMT promoter methylation is the other marker you'll hear about every day. It is prognostic and associated with greater benefit from temozolomide, although that predictive link is not absolute.

How CNS Tumors Present

SymptomWhat it suggests
Headache worse in the morning or lying down, with nausea or vomitingRaised intracranial pressure (mass effect, edema, hydrocephalus)
SeizureA cortical tumor, especially a lower-grade glioma
Focal deficit (weakness, aphasia, visual field cut)Localizes the lesion (see Neuroanatomy)
Personality or cognitive changeFrontal lobe or corpus callosum
Hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalanceVestibular schwannoma
Bitemporal visual loss, hormone problemsPituitary adenoma or craniopharyngioma pressing on the chiasm
Back pain with leg weakness or bladder/bowel change in a cancer patientSpinal cord compression: an emergency
Self-check: a patient with metastatic melanoma has a sudden severe headache and a new brain lesion that is bright on CT. What happened?▾

A hemorrhagic metastasis. Melanoma, renal cell, choriocarcinoma, and thyroid cancer metastases tend to bleed.

High-Yield Summary
  • The first question for any CNS lesion is whether it started in the CNS or spread there, because primary tumors and metastases follow different workups.
  • Brain metastases are the most common intracranial tumor, meningioma is the most common primary tumor, and glioblastoma is the most common malignant primary.
  • Prior radiation is the only established environmental risk factor, and immunosuppression raises the risk of primary CNS lymphoma.
  • Adult diffuse gliomas are classified by IDH and 1p/19q status, and an IDH-wildtype tumor is called glioblastoma only when it meets specific criteria.
  • MGMT promoter methylation is prognostic and associated with greater benefit from temozolomide, although that link is not absolute.

Neuroanatomy.title: Neuroanatomy & Radiation Anatomy: Where Is It?
Neuroanatomy.html:
The question here is where is it, and what is it next to? You need just enough anatomy to localize a lesion from the symptoms, recognize the structures on an MRI, and know which nearby structures will limit the radiation plan. This is not a neuroanatomy course: every structure below is here because it changes either the diagnosis or the plan.

The Big Picture: Lobes, Midline, and Underside

The Lobes and What They Do

  • Each hemisphere has four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital. The central sulcus separates frontal from parietal; the lateral (Sylvian) fissure separates the temporal lobe below.
  • The precentral gyrus is the motor strip; the postcentral gyrus just behind it is the sensory strip. A tumor here is "eloquent": resecting it risks weakness or numbness.
  • Each hemisphere runs the opposite side of the body. The cerebellum is the exception: it controls the same side.
  • Language lives in the dominant hemisphere (the left in almost all right-handed people): Broca's area (frontal) to speak, Wernicke's area (temporal) to understand.

Localizing a Lesion

LocationFunctionA lesion causes
FrontalExecutive function, personality, motor strip, Broca's (dominant)Personality change, contralateral weakness, expressive aphasia, seizures
ParietalSensory strip, spatial awarenessContralateral numbness, neglect (non-dominant)
TemporalHearing, Wernicke's (dominant), memory (hippocampus)Receptive aphasia, memory loss, seizures
OccipitalVisionContralateral homonymous hemianopia
CerebellumCoordinationIpsilateral ataxia; hydrocephalus (4th ventricle)
BrainstemCranial nerves, long tracts, consciousnessCrossed signs: cranial nerve palsy + contralateral body weakness

The Midline and the Brainstem

  • The corpus callosum is the bridge between the hemispheres. A tumor that crosses it to the other side is usually a glioblastoma or lymphoma.
  • The thalamus sits deep in the middle; below it, the hypothalamus controls the pituitary hanging beneath it. Radiation near either can cause hormone deficits years later.
  • The brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla) carries the cranial nerve nuclei and every long tract between brain and body, so a small injury causes big deficits. It is one of the most important organs at risk in the head.
Optional: stroke localization (blood supply)▾

The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes (leg), the middle cerebral artery most of the lateral hemisphere (face, arm, language), and the posterior cerebral artery the occipital lobe and thalamus (vision). On imaging, a stroke is wedge-shaped and follows one artery's territory; a tumor doesn't respect territories.

Deep Structures, Coverings, and CSF

Gray Matter, White Matter, and the Deep Nuclei

  • Gray matter is the cell bodies: the cortex on the surface and the deep nuclei (thalamus and basal ganglia) inside. White matter is the wiring between them, and infiltrative gliomas spread along it.
  • The internal capsule is the narrow white matter lane that carries the motor fibers, so a small lesion there causes a large weakness.
  • The hippocampus sits on the inner surface of the temporal lobe. It forms new memories, which is why hippocampal-avoidance whole-brain RT spares it.
  • Tumors in deep structures (thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem) usually can't be removed safely and are biopsied instead.

The Coverings and the Tentorium

  • Three layers of meninges cover the brain and cord: the tough dura, the thin arachnoid, and the pia on the brain surface. CSF flows in the subarachnoid space between the arachnoid and pia.
  • The tentorium splits the skull into the supratentorial space (the cerebrum, where most adult tumors arise) and the posterior fossa (the cerebellum and brainstem, where most childhood tumors arise).
Intra-axial (inside the brain: gliomas, metastases, lymphoma) vs extra-axial (outside it, from the coverings or nerves: meningiomas, schwannomas). That one distinction narrows the differential more than any other.

CSF Flow and Hydrocephalus

1
Lateral ventricles
→
2
3rd ventricle
→
3
Cerebral aqueduct
→
4
4th ventricle
→
5
Subarachnoid space around the brain and cord
  • A posterior fossa mass can block the aqueduct or 4th ventricle and cause obstructive hydrocephalus: headache, vomiting, papilledema. It often needs a shunt or ventriculostomy before anything else.
  • Because CSF bathes the whole brain and spine, tumors that seed it (medulloblastoma, some germ cell tumors, leptomeningeal disease) put the entire CSF space at risk. That's the anatomic reason for craniospinal irradiation.

The Skull Base: Where Small Tumors Sit Next to Critical Structures

Most benign tumors that radiation treats live at the skull base, right next to nerves that can't take much dose. Learn each neighborhood by what's in it.

NeighborhoodTumors thereWhat's next to it
Sella and suprasellar regionPituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, meningiomaOptic chiasm just above; hypothalamus
Cavernous sinus (either side of the sella)Meningioma, invasive pituitary adenomaInternal carotid and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, VI (double vision, facial numbness)
Internal auditory canal and cerebellopontine angleVestibular schwannoma, meningiomaCN VII and VIII, the cochlea, and the brainstem
OrbitOptic nerve sheath meningioma, orbital lymphomaOptic nerve, lens, retina

Organs at Risk: What Each One Protects

You'll contour these on almost every brain plan. Learn them by the function they protect; the exact dose limits live in the Radiation Planning reading.

Organ at riskInjury means
Brainstem and optic nerves / chiasmPermanent neurologic injury or blindness
CochleaHearing loss
HippocampusMemory decline
Pituitary / hypothalamusEndocrine dysfunction
LensCataract
Normal brainRadionecrosis and cognitive effects
Spinal cordMyelopathy

The Spine

  • The cord ends at L1-L2 (conus medullaris); below that is the cauda equina. The thecal sac ends around S2, which sets the bottom of a craniospinal field.
  • Most spine metastases start in the vertebral body and grow back into the epidural space, where they press on the cord. The Workup and Treatment readings turn that into a decision pathway.
  • The spinal cord is an organ at risk in any field that crosses it: head and neck, lung, esophagus, and every spine metastasis.
High-Yield Summary
  • Localize a lesion from its symptoms by lobe, remembering that the cerebellum controls the same side and brainstem lesions cause crossed signs.
  • Intra-axial tumors grow inside the brain and extra-axial tumors grow from its coverings or nerves, which narrows the differential quickly.
  • A posterior fossa mass can block CSF flow and cause obstructive hydrocephalus, and tumors that seed the CSF put the whole brain and spine at risk.
  • Skull base tumors sit next to the optic chiasm, cavernous sinus nerves, cochlea, and brainstem, which is why they are hard to remove and carefully planned.
  • Each organ at risk protects a function: the optic apparatus protects vision, the cochlea hearing, the hippocampus memory, and the pituitary hormones.

Imaging.title: CNS Imaging: What Does It Look Like?
Imaging.html:
MRI with contrast is the workhorse for almost every CNS tumor: it makes the diagnosis look likely, guides surgery, and is the scan we plan on (fused with the planning CT). CT is the fast first scan in the ER and shows bone, calcium, and blood. Advanced MRI and PET help after treatment. The question here is what does it look like? Most CNS diagnoses start with a picture, which is why Imaging comes before Workup.

ModalityThe question it answersWhen you'll see it
MRI brain with/without contrastWhere is it? What does it look like? How many lesions?Every brain tumor; thin-slice for SRS
CT headBlood? Bone? Calcium? Hydrocephalus?The ER first look
MRI spineCord compression? Leptomeningeal or drop metastases?Back pain + neuro symptoms; tumors that spread through CSF
Perfusion, spectroscopy, amino-acid PETTumor or treatment effect?Growing enhancement after RT
Body CT or FDG PET/CTWhere's the primary? Disease elsewhere?Brain metastases; lymphoma staging
Planning CT (simulation)How do I actually deliver the radiation?Every RT course, fused with the MRI
Learn imaging by the question each test answers, not by memorizing every sequence.

MRI Sequences: What Each One Shows

SequenceBright = Main use
T1 post-contrastEnhancing tissue (broken blood-brain barrier)High-grade tumor, metastases, meningioma, schwannoma; usually the GTV
T2 / FLAIRWater: edema and infiltrative tumor (FLAIR suppresses CSF)Low-grade glioma extent; edema; part of the glioma target
DWI / ADCRestricted diffusion (bright DWI, dark ADC)Dense tumors (lymphoma, medulloblastoma), abscess, stroke
SWI / GREDark = blood or calciumHemorrhagic mets, calcified oligodendroglioma
Enhancement means a broken blood-brain barrier, not necessarily viable tumor. Surgery, radiation, and necrosis all enhance too.

Normal Anatomy on MRI: Level by Level

LevelLandmarksWhy it matters for RT
1. Centrum semiovaleWhite matter sheet, motor "hand knob," falx, superior sagittal sinusLeukoencephalopathy after WBRT; parasagittal meningiomas
2. Lateral ventricle bodiesCorpus callosum, caudate, corona radiataCallosal crossing = GBM or lymphoma; periventricular lymphoma
3. Basal ganglia / thalamusInternal capsule, lentiform nucleus, thalamus, insula, 3rd ventricleDeep, unresectable tumors (biopsy only)
4. Midbrain / suprasellarCerebral peduncles, aqueduct, optic chiasm, hippocampi, temporal lobesChiasm and hippocampal sparing
5. Pons / CPAPons, internal auditory canals, cochlea, 4th ventricle, cerebellumVestibular schwannoma, brainstem and cochlea limits
6. Medulla / foramen magnumMedulla, tonsils, clivus, jugular foramenChordoma, glomus tumors, tonsillar herniation
Self-check: on an axial MRI at the level of the internal auditory canals, which three organs at risk would you contour?▾

The brainstem (pons), both cochleae, and the temporal lobes (plus the cerebellum and facial nerve region depending on the target).

Sella, Orbits, and Spine on MRI

  • The pituitary is best seen on thin coronal slices: look for the chiasm above it and the cavernous sinuses on either side.
  • On orbit images, the lens is dark and the vitreous bright on T2; the optic nerves run back to the chiasm.
  • On a sagittal spine MRI, follow the cord down to the conus at L1-L2 and the thecal sac to S2.

Gliomas

High grade
Glioblastoma
  • Thick, irregular ring enhancement around necrosis
  • Lots of FLAIR edema/infiltration
  • Can cross the corpus callosum ("butterfly")
  • Mass effect, midline shift
Low grade
IDH-mutant glioma
  • Non-enhancing, FLAIR-bright, expansile
  • Little edema or mass effect
  • T2-FLAIR mismatch = IDH-mutant astrocytoma
  • Calcification (CT) = oligodendroglioma
  • Get the MRI within 48-72 hours after surgery to judge the extent of resection before postoperative changes set in.
  • That post-op MRI is fused to the planning CT to draw the target (see Radiation Planning & Toxicity).

Brain Metastases and SRS Planning

  • Mets are round, sit at the gray-white junction, and have edema out of proportion to their size. Often multiple.
  • A thin-slice (1-1.5 mm) contrast MRI within ~1-2 weeks of SRS finds more lesions than routine MRI.
  • Hemorrhagic mets: melanoma, renal, choriocarcinoma, thyroid.
  • Count every lesion and note the largest and the total volume: those, more than the count alone, shape the SRS vs whole-brain decision.
Self-check: a ring-enhancing lesion with bright DWI (restricted diffusion) in the center. Tumor or abscess?▾

Central restricted diffusion favors an abscess (pus). A necrotic tumor usually has facilitated (dark) diffusion in the center. Lymphoma restricts diffusion but enhances solidly.

Benign Tumors: Meningioma, Schwannoma, Pituitary

TumorSignature findingsWhat limits RT
MeningiomaExtra-axial, homogeneous enhancement, dural tail, CSF cleft, hyperostosis, calcificationLocation (optic apparatus near skull base tumors)
Vestibular schwannoma"Ice cream cone": widens the IAC and fills the CPA; cystic change when largeCochlea (hearing), brainstem, CN VII
Pituitary macroadenoma"Snowman" sellar/suprasellar mass; compresses the chiasm; cavernous sinus invasionOptic chiasm (just above)
CraniopharyngiomaSuprasellar, cystic + solid + calcified ("motor oil" cyst fluid)Chiasm, hypothalamus; cysts can grow during RT

CT, Treatment Effect, and the Spine

After Radiation: Tumor or Treatment Effect?

The most important imaging lesson in CNS radiation: new or larger enhancement after treatment is not automatically progression. Timing is the first clue.

Early after chemoRT
Pseudoprogression

More enhancement in the first few months after glioblastoma chemoRT, especially MGMT-methylated tumors. It settles on its own, so don't stop treatment for one scan: repeat the MRI.

Months to years later
Radionecrosis vs recurrence

After SRS or high-dose RT, an enlarging enhancing lesion can be necrosis or tumor. Advanced imaging, short-interval MRI, and sometimes surgery sort it out.

Advanced imaging: how perfusion, spectroscopy, and PET help▾
  • Perfusion MRI: tumor has high blood volume (rCBV); necrosis has low.
  • MR spectroscopy: tumor has a high choline-to-NAA ratio.
  • Amino-acid PET: uptake favors tumor.
  • None is perfect, and mixed tumor and necrosis is common. The RANO criteria formalize response assessment for gliomas.

The Spine

  • Back pain + leg weakness or bladder/bowel change in a cancer patient = MRI of the whole spine now (multiple levels are common).
  • The report should tell you whether the cord is compressed (Bilsky) and whether the spine is stable (SINS); the Workup reading explains both.
High-Yield Summary
  • MRI with contrast answers where the lesion is, what it looks like, and how many there are, while CT shows blood, bone, calcium, and hydrocephalus.
  • T1 post-contrast shows enhancing tumor and T2/FLAIR shows edema and infiltrating tumor.
  • Enhancement means a broken blood-brain barrier, not necessarily viable tumor.
  • Pseudoprogression appears early after chemoradiation, while radionecrosis appears months to years later, and both can look like progression.
  • The planning CT is fused with the MRI so the target drawn on the MRI can be used to calculate dose.

Workup & Decision-Making.title: CNS Workup & Decision-Making: How Do I Classify It?
Workup & Decision-Making.html:
There's no adult CNS TNM stage, so instead of a staging system you answer three questions for every brain or spine lesion. Treatment depends on the tumor type and grade, its location and size, how much is left after surgery, and (for metastases) how many lesions there are and what the rest of the cancer is doing.

1
What is it?

Primary or metastatic? For primary tumors: histology, WHO grade, and molecular markers, or a confident imaging diagnosis for classic benign tumors.

2
Where and how big?

Eloquent brain? Next to the chiasm, brainstem, or cochlea? How many lesions, and how much total volume? Hydrocephalus or cord compression?

3
How is the patient?

Performance status (KPS), age, neurologic deficits, and for metastases, extracranial disease and systemic options.

The bottom of this page has the NCCN workup tables and the grading and scoring reference.

Three Different Workflows

Primary brain tumors, brain metastases, and spine metastases are worked up in completely different ways. Decide which one you're in before anything else.

Primary CNS tumor
Tissue drives everything
  1. Diagnosis (resection or biopsy)
  2. Molecular classification
  3. Grade
  4. Extent of resection / residual disease
  5. RT and systemic therapy
Brain metastasis
The whole patient drives it
  1. Known or unknown primary?
  2. Number and total volume of lesions
  3. Symptoms and mass effect
  4. Location
  5. Extracranial disease and prognosis
  6. CNS-active systemic options
  7. Local therapy
Spine metastasis
The cord drives it
  1. Neurologic status
  2. Epidural compression (Bilsky)
  3. Stability (SINS)
  4. Radiosensitivity of the tumor
  5. Surgery vs RT

The Core Workup

  1. History and neuro exam: symptoms, seizures, focal deficits, KPS.
  2. MRI brain with and without contrast (CT first if the patient is unstable or can't have MRI).
  3. Dexamethasone for symptomatic edema, but hold steroids if lymphoma is suspected until after the biopsy. Antiseizure medicine only if the patient has had a seizure.
  4. Tissue: maximal safe resection (diagnosis and treatment at once) or stereotactic biopsy for deep or eloquent tumors. Classic-looking meningiomas and schwannomas are often treated on imaging alone.
  5. Molecular testing for gliomas: IDH, 1p/19q, and MGMT, plus other markers that refine the diagnosis.
  6. Site-specific extras: body CT or PET for metastases; audiogram for vestibular schwannoma; visual fields and pituitary hormones for sellar tumors; spine MRI and CSF cytology for tumors that spread through CSF; eye exam and HIV test for lymphoma.

Primary Tumors: The Integrated Diagnosis

For adult-type diffuse gliomas, IDH status and other molecular features determine the integrated diagnosis. IDH-mutant tumors are separated by 1p/19q status; qualifying IDH-wildtype tumors may be classified as glioblastoma.

TumorMolecular coreWhat it means clinically
OligodendrogliomaIDH-mutant + 1p/19q codeletedBest prognosis; very chemo-sensitive (PCV)
Astrocytoma, IDH-mutantIDH-mutant, no codeletionYounger adults; grade 2 to 4
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtypeIDH-wildtype + histologic or molecular criteriaAggressive; Stupp regimen for fit patients
  • Grade reflects how aggressive the tumor looks, and some molecular findings can raise it. The details are in the reference box below.
  • MGMT promoter methylation is prognostic and associated with greater benefit from temozolomide, but unmethylated tumors still get standard treatment in fit patients.
  • IDH mutation is the strongest favorable prognostic factor in gliomas.
Reference: full WHO grading and molecular criteria▾
  • Histologic grading: atypia = grade 2; adding significant mitoses = grade 3; necrosis or microvascular proliferation = grade 4.
  • Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype: an IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumor with necrosis or microvascular proliferation, or with a TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or chromosome +7/−10. A tumor that looks low grade can still be glioblastoma on molecular grounds.
  • Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant is grade 4 with necrosis/microvascular proliferation or CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion, but it is not called glioblastoma.
  • Diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered: pons, thalamus, or spinal cord in children and young adults; grade 4.
Quick check: IDH-mutant, 1p/19q intact, with CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion. Diagnosis?▾

Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 4. The deletion raises the grade, but it isn't called glioblastoma, which is reserved for IDH-wildtype tumors.

Brain Metastases: What Drives the Decision

  • Workup: thin-slice contrast MRI to count every lesion, body staging (CT or PET), and tissue if there's no known cancer or it's been years since the primary.
  • Lesion count matters, but it isn't the only thing. Total intracranial tumor volume, the size and location of each lesion, symptoms and mass effect, performance status, extracranial disease, and the available systemic therapy all shape the plan.
  • Prognosis is estimated with the Graded Prognostic Assessment (GPA); the diagnosis-specific GPA adds cancer type and markers. It helps decide whether aggressive local therapy, whole-brain RT, or supportive care fits the patient.

Spine Metastases: Neurologic Status, Bilsky, and SINS

  • Back pain plus new weakness, numbness, or bladder/bowel change in a cancer patient: give dexamethasone and get an MRI of the entire spine the same day.
  • Bilsky grade measures epidural compression: low grade (bone or epidural disease without cord compression) vs high grade (the cord is compressed).
  • SINS scores mechanical stability. An unstable spine needs a surgeon no matter how radiosensitive the tumor is.
  • Radiosensitivity matters too: lymphoma, myeloma, and breast or prostate cancer respond well to conventional RT; renal cell, melanoma, and sarcoma are relatively radioresistant.
Quick check: a patient with breast cancer has back pain; MRI shows epidural tumor compressing the cord. What comes first?▾

Dexamethasone right away, then a same-day spine surgery and radiation oncology evaluation. This is high-grade (Bilsky 2-3) compression; the next question is stability (SINS) and whether she's a surgical candidate.

Everything Else Radiation Treats

You'll also see these on service. Each is described its own way, and the full grading schemes are in the reference tables below.

EntityHow it's describedWhere RT fits
MeningiomaWHO grade 1-3; extent of resection (Simpson grade)Unresectable, residual, recurrent, or higher-grade tumors
Vestibular schwannomaSize, growth, hearing, brainstem contact (Koos grade)Growing small-to-medium tumors (SRS)
Pituitary adenomaMicro (<1 cm) vs macro; functioning vs nonfunctioningResidual or recurrent tumor after surgery or medicine
CraniopharyngiomaCystic, solid, and calcified suprasellar massAfter limited surgery
Primary CNS lymphomaDiffuse large B-cell; stage the eye, CSF, and bodyConsolidation or when chemo isn't possible
MedulloblastomaSpread through CSF; standard vs high riskCraniospinal RT + boost + chemo
AVM, trigeminal neuralgiaNon-cancer conditionsSRS
Benign CNS tumors are often treated on imaging alone: if it looks like a meningioma or an acoustic neuroma and it's growing, radiation is an option without a biopsy.

NCCN Workup by Tumor

What the NCCN Central Nervous System Cancers Guidelines recommend, simplified for learning. Always check the current guideline for real patients.

ImagingMRI brain with/without contrast (pre-op and within 72 h post-op)
SurgeryMaximal safe resection when feasible; stereotactic biopsy otherwise
PathologyWHO integrated diagnosis: IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT, ATRX, TP53, TERT, EGFR, +7/−10, CDKN2A/B, H3 K27M, BRAF
ImagingMRI brain (thin slices for SRS); body staging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET/CT)
TissueBiopsy/resection if no known primary, long interval, or uncertain diagnosis
AssessNumber, size, and total volume; symptoms; KPS; systemic disease and CNS-active systemic options; neurosurgery input
ImagingMRI with contrast (CT for bone/hyperostosis); DOTATATE PET can help define extent
DiagnosisImaging alone is often enough for small asymptomatic tumors; resection gives WHO grade
UrgentDexamethasone for neurologic deficit; MRI of the entire spine
AssessNeurologic status, Bilsky grade, SINS stability, tumor radiosensitivity, systemic disease
ConsultSpine surgery and radiation oncology the same day
Before biopsyHold corticosteroids if possible
StagingMRI brain, ophthalmology slit-lamp exam, CSF cytology (± MRI spine), body CT or PET, HIV test, ± bone marrow

Grading and Scoring Reference

You don't need to memorize these; know what each one measures and where to find it.

Grade 2Diffuse, atypia, low mitotic activity
Grade 3+ significant mitotic activity (anaplasia)
Grade 4+ necrosis and/or microvascular proliferation, or molecular criteria (IDH-wt: TERT/EGFR/+7−10; IDH-mut astro: CDKN2A/B)
Grade 1Benign; <4 mitoses/10 HPF, no brain invasion
Grade 2Brain invasion, or 4-19 mitoses/10 HPF, or 3 of 5 atypical features; chordoid/clear cell
Grade 3≥20 mitoses/10 HPF, frank anaplasia, TERT promoter mutation, or CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion
Simpson I-VI complete + dura + bone; II complete + dura coagulated; III complete, dura left; IV subtotal; V biopsy
Koos IIntracanalicular
Koos IIInto the CPA, no brainstem contact
Koos IIIFills the CPA, contacts the brainstem
Koos IVCompresses the brainstem (surgery favored)
Age<50 = 1; 50-60 = 0.5; >60 = 0
KPS90-100 = 1; 70-80 = 0.5; <70 = 0
Number of mets1 = 1; 2-3 = 0.5; >3 = 0
Extracranial metsNone = 1; present = 0

Original 2008 GPA. The diagnosis-specific GPA (lung, breast, melanoma, GI, renal) uses different factors by cancer type.

0Bone only
1a / 1b / 1cEpidural, no thecal sac deformity / deforms the sac / touches the cord without compression
2Cord compression, CSF still visible
3Cord compression, no CSF visible
ScoresLocation (junctional levels worst), mechanical pain, lytic vs blastic bone, alignment, vertebral body collapse, posterior element involvement
0-6Stable
7-12Potentially unstable: surgical consult
13-18Unstable: surgical consult
Size<3 cm = 1; 3-6 cm = 2; >6 cm = 3
Eloquent brainNo = 0; yes = 1
Deep venous drainageNo = 0; yes = 1

Grade = sum (I-V). Low-grade AVMs are good SRS or surgical candidates.

High-Yield Summary
  • Adult CNS tumors have no TNM stage, so ask what the tumor is, where it is and how big it is, and how the patient is doing.
  • Primary tumors, brain metastases, and spine metastases follow three different workflows, so decide which one you are in first.
  • For primary tumors, tissue gives the integrated diagnosis from histology plus molecular markers such as IDH, 1p/19q, and MGMT.
  • For brain metastases, lesion number matters, but total volume, location, symptoms, performance status, and systemic disease also shape the plan.
  • For spine metastases, neurologic status, Bilsky compression, SINS stability, and tumor radiosensitivity decide between surgery and radiation.

Treatment Paradigms.title: CNS Treatment Paradigms: How Do I Treat It?
Treatment Paradigms.html:
CNS treatment covers many tumors, but the decisions follow a few questions. Answer them in order and most plans fall into place:

1
Can it be safely removed?

Maximal safe resection comes first for most gliomas, large or symptomatic metastases, and many meningiomas. Deep or eloquent tumors are biopsied instead.

2
How aggressive is it?

Benign: observe, or treat when it grows, causes symptoms, or can't be removed. Malignant: RT ± systemic therapy after surgery or biopsy.

3
Focal, regional, or everywhere?

Small, well-defined targets get focal RT (SRS). Infiltrative tumors get fractionated RT with a margin. Widespread disease gets whole-brain or craniospinal RT.

The Tools

ToolWhat it accomplishes
SurgeryDiagnosis, decompression of mass effect, and maximal safe resection
Fractionated RTTreats infiltrative or locally extensive disease over weeks while limiting injury to nearby normal tissue
SRS / SRTAblates small, well-defined targets in 1-5 sessions with a very steep dose falloff
Whole-brain RT (WBRT)Treats visible and microscopic disease throughout the brain
Craniospinal RT (CSI)Treats the entire CSF compartment, brain and spine
Systemic therapyTreats disease outside the radiation field and, for some drugs, disease in the CNS
Reference: typical dose and fractionation▾
SettingRepresentative examples
Glioblastoma60 Gy in 30 fractions; older or frail patients 40 Gy in 15 or 25 Gy in 5
Lower-grade gliomaGrade 2: 50.4-54 Gy; grade 3: 59.4 Gy
MeningiomaFractionated 50.4-54 Gy (grade 1), about 60 Gy (grade 2-3); SRS 12-14 Gy
Vestibular schwannomaSRS 12-13 Gy marginal dose, or fractionated
Pituitary adenomaFractionated 45-54 Gy; SRS about 14-16 Gy (nonfunctioning) to 20-25 Gy (functioning)
Brain metastasis SRSSingle fraction 15-24 Gy by size (RTOG 90-05: ≤2 cm 24 Gy, 2-3 cm 18 Gy, 3-4 cm 15 Gy); larger lesions and cavities 27 Gy in 3 or 30 Gy in 5
WBRT30 Gy in 10 or 20 Gy in 5
Medulloblastoma CSI23.4 Gy (standard risk) or 36 Gy (high risk), plus a boost to about 54 Gy
Spinal cord compression8 Gy in 1, 20 Gy in 5, or 30 Gy in 10; SBRT for selected patients

Regimens vary by institution and protocol; learn the pattern, not the menu.

Paradigm 1: Brain Metastases

This is the most important CNS paradigm to know cold. Work through it as an algorithm, in order:

The brain metastasis algorithm

Stop at the first row that fits.

1
Is it…
Symptomatic?
Start steroids for edema. Local therapy should generally not be delayed.
2
Is it…
Large, with mass effect or hydrocephalus (or tissue needed)?
Neurosurgery for resection.
3
Is it…
Resected?
SRS to the cavity.
4
Is it…
Limited, safely treatable disease?
SRS (± surgery for a dominant lesion).
5
Is it…
Extensive, with a reasonable prognosis?
Hippocampal-avoidance WBRT + memantine, or SRS in selected patients.
6
Is the…
Prognosis poor?
Consider supportive care (steroids) rather than automatically giving WBRT.
7
Is it…
Asymptomatic, with a CNS-active systemic option?
Multidisciplinary discussion about whether local therapy can be safely deferred with close MRI monitoring.

What Decides SRS

SRS alone is preferred for many patients with limited, safely treatable brain metastases. Lesion number matters, but so do total intracranial volume, lesion size and location, symptoms, prognosis, and systemic therapy options. Guidelines support SRS alone for 1-4 unresected metastases in appropriate patients and consider it for 5-10 in selected patients with good performance status.

  • Don't routinely add WBRT to SRS. It improves intracranial control but costs cognition without improving survival, so patients get close MRI follow-up instead and new lesions get more SRS.
  • The main late risk of SRS is radionecrosis, more likely with larger lesions.
  • CNS-active systemic therapy (for example, targeted therapy for EGFR- or ALK-driven lung cancer, HER2-directed therapy, or immunotherapy for melanoma) can shrink brain metastases, but deferring radiation is a selected, case-by-case decision, not a rule.
  • Small cell lung cancer and leptomeningeal disease behave differently: they spread widely, so treatment is more often whole-brain, focal palliative, or (in selected patients) craniospinal.
Limited, good prognosis
SRS

Targets only visible lesions; protects cognition; needs MRI every few months.

Extensive, reasonable prognosis
HA-WBRT + memantine

Treats the whole brain while sparing the hippocampi to protect memory.

Poor prognosis
Supportive care

Steroids and symptom control; WBRT adds little for patients with very short survival (QUARTZ).

NCCTG N0574

Adding WBRT to SRS caused more cognitive decline without improving survival, so limited metastases get SRS alone.

Mahajan & N107C

After resection, cavity SRS improved local control over observation and preserved cognition better than WBRT, making it the standard.

NRG CC001

When WBRT is needed, hippocampal avoidance plus memantine protects memory better than WBRT plus memantine.

JLGK0901

Selected patients with 5-10 small metastases did as well after SRS as those with 2-4, so SRS isn't limited to a fixed count.

Paradigm 2: Glioblastoma

1
Maximal safe resection (or biopsy)
→
2
Fractionated RT + concurrent temozolomide
→
3
Adjuvant temozolomide
  • The Stupp trial established postoperative RT with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide as standard therapy for fit patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma.
  • MGMT methylation means a greater likelihood of benefit from temozolomide. Unmethylated tumors benefit less, but fit patients still get the standard regimen (or a trial).
  • Older or frail patients get shorter RT courses, with or without temozolomide; very frail patients with MGMT-methylated tumors may get temozolomide alone.
  • Glioblastoma almost always recurs. Options at recurrence (re-resection, re-irradiation, systemic therapy, trials) are individualized.
Stupp (EORTC/NCIC)

Adding concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide to RT improved survival in glioblastoma, making RT + TMZ the standard.

Stupp trial and planning details▾
  • Stupp: median survival 14.6 vs 12.1 months; 5-year survival about 10% vs 2%. Regimen: 60 Gy in 30 fractions with daily temozolomide, then 6 cycles of adjuvant temozolomide.
  • Tumor treating fields (EF-14) added to adjuvant temozolomide improved survival further.
  • Older patients: 40 Gy in 15 + temozolomide (Perry) beat RT alone; 25 Gy in 5 matched 40 Gy in 15 (Roa).
  • Target volumes are in the Radiation Planning reading.
Try it: 58-year-old, glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, MGMT unmethylated, gross total resection, KPS 90. Plan?▾

RT with concurrent temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide. Unmethylated tumors get less from temozolomide, but the Stupp regimen is still standard for a fit patient (a trial is also reasonable).

Paradigm 3: Lower-Grade Gliomas

Lower-grade gliomas can behave very differently from glioblastoma, and patients often live many years. Treatment is driven by molecular type, grade, residual disease, age, symptoms, and risk of progression.

Grade 2, lower risk
Observe or selected systemic therapy

Young, well-resected, few symptoms: MRI surveillance, or an IDH inhibitor (vorasidenib) for residual or recurrent IDH-mutant tumors to delay RT and chemo.

Grade 2, higher risk
RT + chemotherapy

Older, subtotal resection, or uncontrolled symptoms: RT followed by chemotherapy (PCV or temozolomide).

Grade 3
RT + chemotherapy

Oligodendroglioma: RT + PCV. Astrocytoma: RT + temozolomide. IDH-mutant grade 4 astrocytoma is treated like glioblastoma.

  • Because these patients live years to decades, late effects on memory, fatigue, and hormones matter, so sparing the hippocampi and normal brain is a real planning goal.
RTOG 9802

Adding PCV chemotherapy to RT for high-risk grade 2 glioma substantially improved overall survival.

INDIGO

Vorasidenib delayed progression in selected IDH-mutant grade 2 gliomas with residual or recurrent disease, postponing RT and chemo.

Reference: the trials behind grade 3 treatment▾
  • RTOG 9402 and EORTC 26951: RT + PCV improved survival for codeleted (oligodendroglial) grade 3 tumors.
  • CATNON: adjuvant temozolomide after RT improved survival for grade 3 astrocytomas without codeletion, mostly in IDH-mutant tumors.
  • RTOG 9802 long-term results: median overall survival about 13 vs 8 years. INDIGO: progression-free survival about 28 vs 11 months.

Paradigm 4: Meningioma

Benign doesn't mean "no radiation." The question is: can I safely remove it, and if not, can I control it with radiation?

  • Small and asymptomatic: observe with serial MRI.
  • Symptomatic or growing, and accessible: surgery.
  • Radiation when surgery can't safely remove it or doesn't finish the job: cavernous sinus and skull base tumors, tumors near the optic apparatus, residual or recurrent disease, and higher-grade tumors.
  • Choosing the technique: small and well separated from critical structures → SRS; larger, or close to the optic nerves or chiasm → fractionated RT.
  • Grade 2: RT is generally favored after subtotal resection; after gross total resection, observation vs RT is still being studied. Grade 3: RT after surgery regardless of resection.

Paradigm 5: Vestibular Schwannoma

The decision is observe vs SRS vs surgery, based on size, growth, hearing, symptoms, and brainstem compression.

Small / not growing
Observe

Serial MRI and audiograms. Many never grow.

Growing, small to medium
SRS

High tumor control with a noninvasive treatment. Hearing can decline over years; facial nerve injury is rare.

Large / compressing the brainstem
Surgery

Mass effect or hydrocephalus. Surgery also fits selected patient preferences and anatomy.

  • For selected small-to-medium tumors, SRS offers high control without an operation; surgery remains important for large tumors, mass effect, and selected patients.
  • Expect temporary swelling in the first year or two after SRS; it isn't failure.
Planning pearl: the cochlea▾

Keeping the cochlea mean dose low (often ≤4 Gy with single-fraction SRS) is associated with better hearing preservation. Marginal SRS dose is usually 12-13 Gy.

Paradigm 6: Pituitary Adenoma and Craniopharyngioma

  • Prolactinoma: cabergoline first, even for large tumors.
  • Other adenomas: transsphenoidal surgery; RT for residual or recurrent tumor or persistent hormone excess. Hormone levels fall slowly after RT (years).
  • The optic chiasm is the critical constraint. SRS is only safe when there's enough distance between the tumor and the chiasm; otherwise use fractionated RT.
  • Hypopituitarism is the main late effect: lifelong endocrine follow-up.
  • Craniopharyngioma: limited surgery (spare the hypothalamus) + RT in selected cases. Cysts can grow during RT, so repeat imaging.

Paradigm 7: Lymphoma and CSF-Spreading Tumors

Primary CNS Lymphoma

High-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy first. WBRT is used for consolidation or when chemo isn't possible; neurotoxicity is a major concern in older patients.

Medulloblastoma

Resection, then craniospinal RT with a boost and chemotherapy. Protons reduce dose to the heart, gut, and growing bones.

Functional SRS

AVMs (obliteration over 2-3 years; bleeding risk persists until then) and trigeminal neuralgia (pain relief over weeks to months).

Paradigm 8: The Spine Emergency

Metastatic spinal cord compression is the CNS emergency you'll be paged about. Walk the algorithm:

Cancer + back pain

Ambulatory status before treatment is the strongest predictor of walking afterward, so move fast.

1
Any…
Neurologic symptoms?
Dexamethasone and MRI of the whole spine now.
2
Is there…
Epidural cord compression?
Grade it with Bilsky.
3
Is there…
Mechanical instability?
Score it with SINS; instability needs a surgeon.
4
Is the patient a…
Surgical candidate?
Surgery (decompression ± stabilization) + postoperative RT.
5
If…
Not a surgical candidate
Urgent RT + steroids.
6
Is it…
Radioresistant, oligometastatic, or a durable prognosis?
Consider SBRT.
Patchell (2005)

In selected patients with cord compression, surgery followed by RT kept more patients walking than RT alone.

NCCN Treatment by Tumor

These are simplified summaries of the NCCN Central Nervous System Cancers Guidelines for learning. Always check the current guideline for real patients.

ScenarioTreatment
Good KPS, youngerRT 60 Gy/30 + concurrent and adjuvant TMZ ± TTFields
Older, good KPSHypofractionated RT (40 Gy/15) + TMZ, or standard RT + TMZ, or TMZ alone (MGMT-methylated)
Poor KPSHypofractionated RT (e.g., 25 Gy/5), TMZ alone, or palliative/supportive care
GradeTreatment
Grade 2Observation (low risk), vorasidenib (residual/recurrent non-enhancing), or RT + TMZ or PCV (high risk)
Grade 3RT + adjuvant TMZ
Grade 4RT + TMZ
GradeTreatment
Grade 2Observation (low risk), vorasidenib, or RT + PCV (high risk)
Grade 3RT + PCV (or TMZ)
ScenarioTreatment
Limited, safely treatable, good prognosisSRS (preferred) ± surgery for large/symptomatic lesions
After resectionSRS/SRT to the cavity (or WBRT)
Asymptomatic, CNS-active systemic optionSelected patients: systemic therapy with close MRI monitoring, after multidisciplinary discussion
ScenarioTreatment
Reasonable prognosisWBRT with hippocampal avoidance + memantine, or SRS for selected patients
Poor prognosisBest supportive care or short WBRT
ScenarioTreatment
Small, asymptomaticObservation
Symptomatic / growing, accessibleSurgery; RT for residual (grade 1: consider; grade 2: favored if subtotal)
InaccessibleSRS or fractionated RT
Grade 3Surgery + RT
ScenarioTreatment
Cord compression, surgical candidateSurgery + RT
Cord compression, not a surgical candidateRT + steroids
No compression, radioresistant or oligometastaticSBRT
ScenarioTreatment
InductionHigh-dose methotrexate-based regimen
ConsolidationHigh-dose chemo + stem cell rescue, or WBRT (reduced dose after complete response)
Not a chemo candidateWBRT
High-Yield Summary
  • Symptomatic or large brain metastases need prompt local therapy, often surgery followed by SRS to the cavity.
  • SRS alone is preferred for many patients with limited, safely treatable brain metastases, and whole-brain RT is not routinely added.
  • Extensive brain metastases with a reasonable prognosis get hippocampal-avoidance whole-brain RT with memantine, while a poor prognosis may call for supportive care instead.
  • Glioblastoma is treated with maximal safe resection followed by RT with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide, with shorter courses for older or frail patients.
  • Meningiomas and other benign tumors are observed, removed, or treated with radiation when they cannot be safely removed, and spinal cord compression gets steroids plus surgery and RT or urgent RT alone.

Radiation Planning & Toxicity.title: CNS Radiation Planning & Toxicity: How Do I Deliver It Safely?
Radiation Planning & Toxicity.html:
The last question is the one that makes this a radiation oncology rotation: how does the MRI become a treatment plan, and how do you deliver it safely? Every CNS plan follows the same four steps, then the same toxicity logic: each organ at risk you protect maps to a side effect you'll counsel the patient about.

From MRI to Treatment Plan

1
Simulate and fuse

The patient is immobilized (a thermoplastic mask, or a frame for some SRS) and gets a planning CT. The MRI is fused to it: MRI shows the tumor and anatomy; CT gives the electron density needed to calculate dose.

2
Define the target

GTV: visible disease or the resection cavity. CTV: the region at risk for microscopic spread, when appropriate. PTV: a margin for setup uncertainty.

3
Identify the OARs

Which ones depend on location: optic apparatus, brainstem, cochlea, hippocampus, pituitary, lens, spinal cord.

4
Choose the technique

Match the technique to the shape of the disease (table below).

Use the most recent MRI. Brain metastases grow and new ones appear, so an SRS plan is built on a thin-slice contrast MRI taken shortly before treatment.

Choosing the Technique

Shape of the diseaseTechniqueExamples
Small, well-defined focal targetSRS / SRTBrain metastases, resection cavities, vestibular schwannoma, small meningioma
Infiltrative tumor with microscopic spreadFractionated RT (IMRT/VMAT, sometimes protons)Glioblastoma, lower-grade glioma, large or optic-adjacent meningioma
Diffuse intracranial diseaseWBRT, ideally with hippocampal avoidanceExtensive brain metastases, some lymphoma
Disease spread through CSFCraniospinal irradiationMedulloblastoma, some germ cell tumors, selected leptomeningeal disease

Fractionation is the lever when a target sits next to a critical structure: spreading the dose over more sessions lets the nearby nerve repair between treatments. That's why a meningioma touching the chiasm is treated over weeks instead of in one SRS session.

Defining the Target: Two Contrasting Plans

The biggest planning difference between CNS tumors is whether there's a CTV. A metastasis is a well-defined ball that pushes brain aside; a glioma infiltrates along white matter beyond what you can see.

Brain Metastasis SRS

PTVGTV plus a very small margin (often 0-2 mm)
GTVThe enhancing lesion on thin-slice T1 post-contrast MRI (or the cavity after resection); no CTV for an intact metastasis
While protecting
  • Normal brain (radionecrosis)
  • Brainstem
  • Optic apparatus
  • Cochlea, when nearby

Glioblastoma

PTVCTV plus a setup margin
CTVA margin for infiltrating tumor cells, trimmed at anatomic barriers (skull, falx, tentorium, ventricles)
GTVEnhancing tumor plus the resection cavity on post-op MRI (± FLAIR abnormality)
While protecting
  • Brainstem
  • Optic nerves and chiasm
  • Hippocampi (when feasible)
  • Cochlea
  • Lenses and retina
  • Pituitary
Planning details: glioma margins and imaging timing▾
  • Post-op MRI within about 48-72 hours shows the extent of resection before postoperative changes set in; the planning MRI is repeated closer to RT if there's been a delay.
  • Glioblastoma CTV is commonly the GTV plus about 1.5-2 cm, trimmed at barriers. Some groups use a two-phase plan: FLAIR abnormality to about 46 Gy, then a boost to the enhancing tumor and cavity to 60 Gy.
  • Lower-grade gliomas are usually non-enhancing, so the GTV is the T2/FLAIR abnormality, with a smaller CTV margin.
  • Protocols differ in margin size; follow the institutional or trial protocol.

Organs at Risk: What Each One Protects

Organ at riskInjury looks likeWhen it matters most
Brainstem / optic apparatusNeurologic injury; vision lossSkull base meningioma, pituitary, posterior fossa tumors
CochleaHearing lossVestibular schwannoma, CPA and temporal tumors
HippocampusMemory declineWhole-brain RT; long-term survivors of lower-grade glioma
Pituitary / hypothalamusEndocrine dysfunction (often years later)Sellar tumors; any plan near the midline skull base
Normal brainRadionecrosis, cognitive effectsSRS (especially larger targets), re-irradiation
Lens / retinaCataract / retinopathyOrbit and frontal skull base
Spinal cordMyelopathySpine metastases, craniospinal RT
Planning reference: commonly used dose constraints▾
OrganConventional fractionationSingle-fraction SRS
Optic nerves / chiasmMax about 54 GyMax about 8-10 Gy
BrainstemMax about 54 Gy (small volumes higher by protocol)Max about 12-15 Gy
Spinal cordMax about 45-50 GyPer SBRT protocol
CochleaMean about 35-45 GyMean often ≤4 Gy (schwannoma)
Normal brain Volume receiving 12 Gy (V12) predicts radionecrosis
Hippocampi (HA-WBRT)Kept far below the whole-brain dose per protocol 
LensMax about 7-10 Gy 

Representative values only; constraints vary by protocol, fractionation, and clinical situation.

Toxicity by Timing

Acute (during RT)
  • Fatigue
  • Hair loss in the field
  • Scalp redness
  • Headache, nausea, or worse deficits from edema (steroids help)
Early delayed (weeks to months)
  • Somnolence and fatigue after whole-brain RT
  • Pseudoprogression after glioma chemoRT
  • Temporary swelling after schwannoma or meningioma SRS
Late (months to years)
  • Radionecrosis
  • Cognitive decline and memory loss
  • Hypopituitarism
  • Hearing loss, vision loss, cataract
  • Secondary tumors (rare; mostly in children and long-term survivors)

Radionecrosis

  • An enhancing, often enlarging lesion months to years after SRS or high-dose RT. It can look exactly like recurrence; the Imaging reading covers how to tell them apart.
  • Risk rises with larger targets, higher dose, re-irradiation, and possibly with some systemic therapies.
  • Asymptomatic necrosis can be watched. Symptomatic necrosis is treated with steroids, then bevacizumab or laser ablation, or surgery if needed.
Clinical Pearl

When you counsel a patient before brain RT, the plan tells you what to say: an SRS patient hears about radionecrosis and close MRI follow-up; a WBRT patient hears about fatigue and memory; a sellar tumor patient hears about lifelong hormone checks.

High-Yield Summary
  • Every CNS plan fuses the MRI to a planning CT, defines the target, identifies the nearby organs at risk, and chooses a technique.
  • Small focal targets get SRS, infiltrative tumors get fractionated RT, diffuse intracranial disease gets whole-brain RT, and CSF spread gets craniospinal RT.
  • A glioma plan includes a CTV for microscopic infiltration, while an intact metastasis treated with SRS usually does not.
  • Fractionation protects nearby nerves, which is why tumors close to the optic chiasm are treated over several weeks.
  • Late effects include radionecrosis, cognitive decline, hypopituitarism, and hearing or vision loss, and symptomatic radionecrosis is treated first with steroids.
